newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - UK non-life market undifferentiated.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - UK non-life market undifferentiated.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN

Swiss Re's survey of consumer attitudes in the UK non-life insurance market last week gives personal lines insurers around the world an interesting insight on branding - particularly those now coping with deregulated markets.

The UK market is complex in its variety of distribution and stuffed with players, and yet the absence of real differentiation continues. Perhaps that's why 84 per cent of consumers in the Swiss Re survey said they found the choice between them confusing.
Price is of course very important, but consumer sense of security and trust in brands is also growing in importance.

In many ways this is a return to the idea which prevailed before Direct Line shook the market up in 1985. The difference is that it is not the insurance companies which have the best brands - but those such as supermarket chains Tesco and Marks & Spencer, or multi-business conglomerates such as Virgin, who have decided to try selling insurance as well.
Consumers are increasingly open to the idea of buying insurance from them, and traditional insurers will be forced to tackle them at their own game.

In the survey, 64 per cent of consumers agreed there were only a few well known companies they can rely on in the non-life market. This means providers a) have to secure a place on the consumers 'quote list', and b) be sufficiently differentiated from the others to be the one ultimately chosen.

Brands help people short circuit the time consuming process of assessing the wide range of choices. Insurers therefore now have to look to their own brand image as much as soft drink manufacturers, because soft-drink manufacturers are starting to sell insurance.
--oo0oo--
While the insurance industry debates whether risk securitisation will take off, it is becoming increasingly clear that investors have already made up their minds.
The issue of United Services Automobile Association hurricane bonds, which recently closed ahead of schedule had almost $1 billion offered for a maximum placement of $400m.
Perhaps more significant is that while protected notes were two times oversubscribed, unprotected notes were 10 times oversubscribed.

Insurers and reinsurers have argued about whether there is enough demand from insurance customers for these products on a wide scale. But the indication is that there is plenty of demand for them as investment opportunities among hedge funds and institutions.

This element of these multi-faceted transactions may well prove to be a driving force, rather than insurers. If that means these products becoming cheaper and offer more clear-cut alternatives to traditional products, those insurers who have been in at the start will benefit most.
